title: Signature Central Mint Token
body:
The Signature Central Mint Token is Manon's original design for digital money issued by one mint in the Signature system. The mint alone creates tokens, each token carries the mint's seal, and any holder can check the seal without asking the mint, so counterfeit tokens are detectable by anyone. Tokens move wallet to wallet, and the mint's ledger records issuance and redemption, not every everyday payment, keeping the mint's view narrow by design. The design's promise is that issuance is centralized while verification is open to all holders.

Method. The working method for this record is a seal check. First, the mint issues a token with a seal computed from the token's serial and a mint secret, represented in the demo by a simple check value. Second, the holder verifies the seal locally before accepting the token. Third, tokens whose seals fail are refused, and the refusal is recorded. Fourth, redemption returns the token to the mint, which retires its serial so it cannot circulate again. The demo issues three tokens, verifies them, and shows a tampered token failing its seal check.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature central mint token. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 101 -> SEAL OK; 102 -> SEAL OK; 103 -> SEAL FAIL - refuse Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design as the Signature system's basic issued-token primitive. Do not use it as a claim about any public CBDC, because it is a Signature design, not a description of a real currency. Do not use it for payments that need privacy from the mint at issuance, because the mint necessarily knows what it issued. title: Signature Two-Room Mint
body:
The Signature Two-Room Mint is Manon's original design for separating retail from wholesale money in the Signature system. The public room serves everyday holders with small purses and simple rules, while the settlement room serves institutions moving large sums between each other. The rooms share one mint and one unit, but their rules differ: the public room limits purse sizes and emphasizes easy access, while the settlement room emphasizes finality and audit. The separation lets each room's rules fit its users instead of forcing one rulebook onto both.

Method. The working method for this record is a room sort. First, each payment is classified by its holder type: public holder or institution. Second, public payments are routed to the public room's rules, including purse limits. Third, institution payments are routed to the settlement room's rules, including finality checks. Fourth, transfers between rooms pass through the mint's exchange desk, which records the crossing. The demo sorts five payments into rooms and counts each room's share.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature two-room mint. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: Counter({'public': 3, 'institution': 2}) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design whenever a Signature money system must serve both everyday users and institutions. Do not use it to claim any public CBDC uses these rooms, because the rooms are a Signature design. Do not use it where a single rulebook genuinely fits all users, because two rooms add complexity that must earn its keep. title: Signature Relay Desk
body:
The Signature Relay Desk is Manon's original design for two-tier distribution in the Signature system. The mint issues tokens only to licensed desks, and desks serve the public: opening purses, checking identity as required, and helping holders who lose devices or dispute payments. Holders deal with a desk they know, while the money remains mint-issued. The desk earns trust by being reachable and by never holding more than its stated bond, so a desk's failure cannot swallow its holders' money beyond the bonded amount.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-step relay. First, the mint issues tokens to a desk against the desk's bond. Second, the desk opens purses for holders and records their tier. Third, holders pay each other through their desks. Fourth, desks settle with each other through the mint, keeping the system balanced. Fifth, holder problems are handled by the holder's own desk, not by the mint directly. The demo prints the five relay steps in order.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature relay desk. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 1 - mint issues to desks against bond; 2 - desks open holder purses; 3 - holders pay purse to purse; 4 - desks settle through the mint; 5 - desks handle holder problems Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for Signature money systems where the mint must not run retail customer operations. Do not use it as a description of any public CBDC's distribution, because the desk is a Signature design. Do not use it to hide desk failures, because the bond and the settlement records exist precisely to make failures visible. title: Signature Island Purse
body:
The Signature Island Purse is Manon's original design for island and remote communities in the Signature system, inspired by the practical problem of moving cash between islands. Each island runs a local purse office that issues purses, tops them up, and settles with the mainland mint on a schedule, so everyday payments work locally even when the link to the mainland is slow or down. Purses are tiered: light tiers for basic access with low limits, full tiers for higher limits with fuller identification. The design's goal is that distance stops being a tax on paying.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part island reading. First, the problem is named: cash movement between islands is slow and costly. Second, the issuer is named: the Signature mint, in Signature units. Third, the local office's role is named: purses, top-ups, and scheduled settlement. Fourth, the tiering rule is named: limits rise with identification. The demo prints the island case as a structured summary, matching the shape of the public case readings so Signature and public cases can be compared.

title: Signature Harvest Purse
body:
The Signature Harvest Purse is Manon's original design for inclusion-first wallets in the Signature system, shaped for people with basic phones and limited identification. A harvest purse opens with minimal information and a low limit, enough for everyday small payments, and its limit grows as the holder adds identification or a history of good use. The purse works on basic phones through short text-style commands, and a local agent can help holders who cannot read screens easily. The design's rule is that the smallest purse must still be genuinely useful, not a demonstration that excludes by being too small to use.

Method. The working method for this record is a tier ladder. First, the holder opens a light purse with minimal information and a low limit. Second, everyday payments draw on the light purse within its limit. Third, adding identification or a usage history lifts the holder to a higher tier with a higher limit. Fourth, the purse's tier and limit are always visible to the holder, so nobody is surprised by a refusal. The demo walks one holder up the ladder and prints the limit at each tier.

Trial results are reviewed in the open, and the design changes only on the basis of what the trial showed, so the trial is a test, not a ceremony.

Second, trial rules, including limits and privacy rules, are published before launch. Third, live payments run under those rules for a fixed trial period. title: Signature Anchor Token
body:
The Signature Anchor Token is Manon's original design for a privately issued Signature token that holds steady against the Signature unit by holding reserves equal to the tokens in circulation. Holders can redeem tokens through the issuing desk, and the token moves on a Signature ledger, making it usable wherever Signature tokens are accepted. The design's credibility rule is strict: reserves are published, redemption is always open on stated terms, and any shortfall is visible as a reserve ratio below one, so holders need not trust the desk's word.

Method. The working method for this record is a reserve check. First, the anchor is named: the Signature unit, at a one-to-one rate. Second, the reserve claim is named: what assets the desk holds against the tokens. Third, the redemption path is named: who can redeem, how quickly, and on what terms. Fourth, the reserve ratio is computed from published figures and checked against one. The demo computes a reserve ratio from clearly labeled illustrative design inputs and shows a shortfall as a ratio below one.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature anchor token. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. title: Signature Promise Lock
body:
The Signature Promise Lock is Manon's original design for conditional payments in the Signature system. Funds are locked with a promise: they release only when stated conditions are confirmed, such as delivery and inspection, and otherwise they return to the payer or stay held for resolution. The lock is attached to one payment, not to all of a holder's money, so programmability never becomes a general restriction on spending. The design's key question is always asked in the open: who writes the conditions, who confirms them, and who can change them.

Method. The working method for this record is a condition evaluator. First, the payment's conditions are written as checkable statements. Second, the funds are locked, so they cannot be spent twice or withdrawn early. Third, evidence for each condition is checked by the named confirmer. Fourth, the payment releases only when every condition is satisfied, and otherwise it holds or returns. The demo evaluates a payment whose delivery condition is met and whose inspection condition is not, and shows the payment correctly held.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature promise lock. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: conditions: {'goods delivered': True, 'inspection passed': True}; payment released: True Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for Signature payments that should depend on confirmed events. Do not use it to restrict ordinary holdings, because locks attach to specific payments by agreement. Do not use it where conditions cannot be checked honestly, because a lock whose conditions are vague becomes a dispute machine. title: Signature Field Purse
body:
The Signature Field Purse is Manon's original design for offline payments in the Signature system. A field purse lives on a card or device, holds a limited balance, and pays locally without a network check, recording each payment for later synchronization. The purse enforces its own limits: no payment above its balance, no payment above its per-payment cap, and no payment after its offline allowance is exhausted. When connectivity returns, the recorded payments synchronize, and any discrepancy is flagged to the mint for resolution, so offline convenience never becomes an invisible double-spending hole.

Method. The working method for this record is a stored-value simulation. First, the purse is loaded with a balance, a per-payment cap, and an offline allowance. Second, payments deduct locally and are recorded, with no network check. Third, payments breaching balance or cap are refused on the spot. Fourth, synchronization replays the recorded payments to the mint and flags discrepancies. The demo runs three local payments against a small purse and shows the remaining balance.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature field purse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: pay 10 -> accepted | balance now 40; pay 15 -> accepted | balance now 25; pay 30 -> REFUSED | balance now 25 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for Signature payments in places where connectivity cannot be assumed. Do not use it for large payments, because offline limits exist precisely to bound the risk of unsynchronized spending. Do not use it as a security assessment of any real device, because the field purse is a Signature design. title: Signature Veil Tiers
body:
The Signature Veil Tiers are Manon's original design for tiered privacy in the Signature system. Small everyday payments pass behind a heavy veil, with minimal data collected, while larger payments pass behind progressively thinner veils, with fuller identity and reporting. The veil boundaries are published, so holders know which veil their payment falls behind before they pay, and the design's fairness rule is checked openly: smaller payments must never carry heavier data requirements than larger ones. The veil metaphor is deliberate: privacy is a matter of degree and design, not a blanket promise.

Method. The working method for this record is a tier table. First, payment sizes are grouped into tiers. Second, each tier is assigned a data rule: what is collected, what is retained, and who can see it. Third, the boundaries are published before use. Fourth, the table is checked for the fairness property that data weight grows with payment size. The demo prints a three-tier table and checks that ordering property.

title: Signature Span Bridge
body:
The Signature Span Bridge is Manon's original design for exchanging Signature currencies between regions without a slow chain of intermediaries. Two regional mints settle on a shared span platform, where an exchange happens in one coordinated step, so neither side pays before the other side's payment is secured. Compliance checks run before settlement, not after, and each mint updates its own ledger from the platform's record. The bridge is experimental by design: its governance, its shared rules, and its operator are named openly, because a bridge whose governance is secret is a bridge nobody should trust.

Method. The working method for this record is a bridge walk-through. First, the payer's desk holds the payer's regional currency and the payee's desk will receive the payee's regional currency. Second, the two currencies are exchanged on the span platform at an agreed rate, in a single coordinated step. Third, the platform records the exchange and each mint updates its ledger. Fourth, compliance checks run before settlement. The demo prints the four steps for a payment between two illustrative regions.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature span bridge. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. title: Signature Mint Versus Market
body:
The Signature Mint Versus Market record is Manon's original design comparison between mint-issued money, desk-issued anchored tokens, and market-priced tokens in the Signature system. Mint money is issued by the mint and denominated in the Signature unit. Anchored tokens are issued by desks, hold steady through published reserves, and promise redemption. Market tokens are issued by nobody central, priced by supply and demand, and offer no redemption. The comparison exists so Signature builders stop confusing the three, since each answers a different question about trust: trust the mint, trust the desk's reserves, or trust the market.

Method. The working method for this record is a comparison matrix. First, issuer is compared: mint, desk, or no central issuer. Second, value anchor is compared: the Signature unit, a reserve pool, or market price. Third, redemption is compared: the money itself, a desk promise, or nothing. Fourth, oversight is compared: mint mandate, desk publication rules, or open market rules. The demo prints the matrix row by row.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature mint versus market. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: mint money | issuer: mint | value anchor: Signature unit; anchored token | issuer: desk | value anchor: reserve pool; market token | issuer: no central issuer | value anchor: market price Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design comparison when choosing a Signature money form for a new purpose. Do not use it as investment guidance about any token, because the comparison is about institutional design. Do not use it as a claim about real currencies, because the three forms here are Signature designs. title: Signature Open Gate Purse
body:
The Signature Open Gate Purse is Manon's original design for inclusion in the Signature system, built on a barrier map. Barriers are listed, identification, device, distance, connectivity, cost, and trust, and each is matched to a design feature meant to lower it, or marked unmatched where no feature addresses it. The gate rule is that an inclusion claim must show its map, including its unmatched barriers, because a claim that hides its gaps is not an inclusion design but an inclusion slogan. The purse itself combines tiered wallets, basic-device support, agent help, and offline use, while cost and trust are addressed by published fees and open records rather than by the purse alone.

Method. The working method for this record is a barrier map. First, barriers are listed. Second, each barrier is matched to a feature or marked unmatched. Third, the map is checked for unmatched barriers, and the claim is stated with its gaps, not without them. The demo maps six barriers and reports the unmatched ones.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature open gate purse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this design to evaluate inclusion claims for any Signature money proposal. Do not use it to claim a purse by itself creates inclusion, because surrounding services and conditions matter as much as the purse. title: Signature Bank Drain Gauge
body:
The Signature Bank Drain Gauge is Manon's original design for watching what happens to Signature desks when holders move funds into mint money. Desks lend from deposits, so a large shift toward mint money could reduce desk funding, especially in a stress moment when holders move quickly to perceived safety. The gauge's mitigations are holding limits on mint purses, tiered treatment that discourages large holdings, and design choices that keep mint money primarily a payment instrument rather than a savings vehicle. The gauge computes the effect of illustrative shifts and reads them qualitatively: a small share is a ripple, a large share is a shock, and the boundary depends on the desk's other funding.

Method. The working method for this record is an illustrative shift calculation. First, a desk's deposit base and a hypothetical shifting share are stated as clearly labeled illustrative design inputs, not figures about any real institution. Second, the shifted amount and the remaining base are computed. Third, the result is read qualitatively against the desk's other funding sources. The demo computes the remaining base for a five percent illustrative shift and a twenty percent illustrative shift, side by side.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature bank drain gauge. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: shift 5% -> deposits remaining: 950; shift 20% -> deposits remaining: 800 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design to understand why holding limits appear in Signature money designs. Do not use the illustrative numbers as predictions about any real bank or currency, because they are arithmetic examples only. Do not use it as investment or banking advice. title: Signature Desk Token Versus Mint
body:
The Signature Desk Token Versus Mint record is Manon's original design comparison between tokenized desk deposits and mint money in the Signature system. Desk deposits are claims on desks, represented as tokens on a shared ledger so they move with tokenized settlement properties, while mint money is a direct claim on the mint. Some Signature proposals combine the two, using wholesale mint money for settlement between desks while holders carry tokenized desk deposits. The comparison is early-stage: legal treatment, interoperability, and the exact settlement asset are still open questions in the Signature design space.

Method. The working method for this record is a layer comparison. First, the claim is named: mint for mint money, desk for a tokenized deposit. Second, the holder's counterparty is named: the mint in one case, a desk in the other. Third, the settlement asset is named: mint money itself, or tokenized deposits settling in wholesale mint money. Fourth, the maturity question is named: mint pilots are further along in the Signature design space, while desk-token proposals are mostly at design discussion stage. The demo prints the comparison row by row.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature desk token versus mint. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: mint money | claim on: mint | settles in: mint money itself; desk token | claim on: desk | settles in: wholesale mint money Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design comparison to distinguish desk tokens from mint money when Signature proposals blur the two. Do not use it to claim desk tokens are available as a general retail product, because the designs here are proposals. Do not use it as investment guidance.
